result.exact_title: SYMPHONY: Improving Memory Management for LLM Inference Workloads
result.date_or_venue: arXiv preprint 2412.16434 (cs.DC), v1 submitted 21 Dec 2024. Only v1 exists and the abs page lists no peer-reviewed venue. Authors: Saurabh Agarwal, Anyong Mao, Aditya Akella, Shivaram Venkataraman.
result.url_checked: https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.16434 ; https://arxiv.org/html/2412.16434v1 (full text downloaded and searched)
result.what_it_actually_does:
Clients send "advisory requests" before the real request: for a chatbot when the user starts typing, and for an agent when the upstream agent sends one to the next agent. The paper's example format has the fields session_id, model_id, expected_arrival, ordered and priority. For chatbots expected_arrival is None. It has a value only for agents (for example 3.2), where it is a lower bound on arrival taken from offline profiling. The paper says the expected arrival time is extra information for the cluster-level scheduler. It never says the node manager uses it.

The scheduler picks a node, which in the paper means even load balancing. It then adds the cache location to the advisory and forwards it. The forwarded advisory carries only two things: the session ID and the current KV location. The node manager acts as soon as that advisory arrives. If the cache is on another node, it fetches it by RPC. If the cache is local, it moves it "subject to memory constraints" to the fastest tier it can: GPU HBM, then host DRAM, then disk. The paper walks through three cases: GPU, host and disk when HBM is plentiful; host and disk only when there is no free HBM; and prefetch into HBM, then evict when memory gets tight.

There is no timing rule for when to prefetch relative to the expected arrival. The node manager "greedily transfers the K,V cache to occupy available GPU memory whenever it is free". The paper also states as a limitation that it "assumes that advisory requests arrive early enough".

When several advisories compete for HBM, blocks are prioritized by layer, lower layers first. Later layers load when the real request arrives, using asynchronous layer-wise reads that overlap with the forward pass.

The paper calls this protection and eviction scheme "cooperative memory management", and it applies only to HBM. Under memory pressure, the serving library (vLLM or TensorRT-LLM) can overwrite or purge prefetched KV blocks. The eviction order is later-layer blocks first, then the smallest KV caches. This costs no data transfer because a copy always stays in host memory and on disk; a background thread keeps disk up to date.

Nothing in the paper models queueing delay or queue wait in any prefetch or eviction decision. The only match for "queue" in the text is the title of a cited reference.
result.corrections:
The substance of the claim is correct: advisory-triggered promotion to the fastest tier, prefetched copies purgeable under pressure, no explicit timing rule, no queue term. The wording overstates one link, though.

(1) The expected arrival is not what drives the node manager's move. The expected_arrival field is optional: it is None for chatbots and a profiled lower bound only for agents. The paper says it gives "the scheduler" extra information. The advisory that reaches the node manager holds only the session ID and the KV location. The node manager promotes the KV greedily as soon as the advisory arrives, subject to free memory, and does not schedule the move against the arrival estimate.

(2) The promotion does not always move the whole session KV to the fastest tier. When HBM is contended, only the lower layers are placed in HBM first. When no HBM is free, the KV goes only to host memory and disk.

(3) The purge is done by the serving framework, under what the paper calls "cooperative memory management", and applies only to HBM. The eviction order is later layers first, then the smallest caches. Copies stay safe in DRAM and on disk.

(4) "No explicit timing rule" and "no queue term" are right. The paper only assumes advisories arrive "early enough" and never models queue wait. The work is an arXiv preprint (v1, Dec 2024) with no listed venue.
quotes: "expected_arrival": None, ... Figure 10: Advisory request for chatbot: The above depicts the format of advisory request for chatbot. Since there is no guarantee about arrival time and ordering these sent with no arrival time and ordering.

"expected_arrival": 3.2, ... Figure 11: Advisory request for Agent: With agent workload with additional profiling we know that we can provide some information about expected arrival time. However, we can not provide any information concerning ordering. The expected arrival time provides the scheduler with additional information to make better scheduling decisions.

An advisory request received from the scheduler contains two pieces of information: the session ID of the expected inference request and the current location of the associated K,V cache. Upon receiving an advisory request, the node manager verifies the cache's location. If the cache resides on a different node, the node manager issues an RPC call to retrieve it. If the cache is locally available, the node manager, subject to memory constraints, moves it to the fastest memory tier possible.

In cooperative memory management, the Symphony node manager greedily transfers the K,V cache to occupy available GPU memory whenever it is free. However, under increased memory pressure, the underlying serving library can overwrite this memory by purging parts of the K,V cache. Since a copy of the K,V cache is already stored in host memory, this operation requires no additional data transfer.

Since K,V cache blocks are overwritten based on their assigned priority. Blocks associated with later layers in the network are given the lowest priority, followed by K,V caches with the smallest size, which are assigned the second-lowest priority. We would like to highlight we use cooperative memory management only for managing GPU HBM.

In Symphony, we always maintain one copy of the K,V cache in the slowest memory hierarchy (disk). This design ensures data persistence, enabling us to perform on-demand evictions from higher memory tiers without risking data loss.

In the above example of multiple advisory requests arriving for different sessions, the priority-based approach would result in KV cache from lower layers of both sessions being moved to HBM, while other layers will be moved once the request arrives.

However, these advisory requests do not provide details about the order of requests or their precise arrival times. In agent workloads, where requests are sent by preceding agents, it is possible to estimate a minimum arrival time.

Symphony assumes that advisory requests arrive early enough to allow sufficient time for K,V cache migrations. However, in extreme cases where there is insufficient time between the advisory request (or there was no advisory request) and the associated inference request, performance may be impacted.
Case 3: No GPU Memory Available. In this case, the Symphony node manager moves the K,V cache for Session ID: 1 to host memory and disk, bypassing the GPU due to lack of available memory.

result.exact_title: PCR: A Prefetch-Enhanced Cache Reuse System for Low-Latency RAG Serving

The HTML still has the unfilled ACM template placeholder ("Conference: Make sure to enter the correct conference title...; June 03–05, 2018; Woodstock, NY"), so it has no confirmed venue. Authors: Wenfeng Wang, Xiaofeng Hou (corresponding author), Peng Tang, Hengyi Zhou, Jing Wang, Xinkai Wang, Chao Li, Minyi Guo, all at Shanghai Jiao Tong University. Footnote: "New Paper, Not an Extension of a Conference Paper."
result.url_checked: https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.23049 ; https://arxiv.org/html/2603.23049 (full text downloaded and grepped verbatim)
result.what_it_actually_does:
PCR is a RAG-focused KV-cache reuse system built on vLLM, not SGLang. Its own Cache Engine manages 256-token KV chunks in CPU DRAM and on SSD using a prefix tree; GPU memory is left to vLLM's block manager (16-token blocks). It has three techniques.

(1) Look-ahead LRU. Only leaf chunks of the prefix tree can be evicted, and they are ordered by LRU. Each step, the vLLM scheduler passes the waiting requests inside a "preloading window" to the cache engine. Their matched chunks get a recency/priority bump (Algorithm 1: "if in CPU cache then BumpPriority(key)"), so they are less likely to be evicted. This is a soft reorder of recency, not a hard pin or refcount. It works at the DRAM (and SSD) chunk level, not on GPU-resident KV.

(2) Queue-based prefetch. In the same pass, if a chunk is on SSD but not in DRAM, it is loaded SSD->CPU asynchronously ("SubmitSSDToCPULoad") by a dedicated Prefetcher thread. The pass walks the chunks in prefix order and stops at the first miss. Requests are walked in reverse order of scheduler_output.prefetch_reqs. The window slides forward after each cycle. Algorithm 1 also calls "EnforcePrefetchWindow" and "ShrinkPrefetchWindow", which are not explained. The trigger signal is membership in the waiting queue. The rationale given is that queued requests have already finished document retrieval, and queueing time is long under heavy load. There is no queue-time or ETA-based timing model: prefetch fires for any request inside the window, and the window size is a static config value.

(3) Layer-wise overlap. CPU->GPU load, compute, and GPU->CPU offload run on three CUDA streams, using cudaMemcpyBatchAsync. New KV is written back to SSD asynchronously.

The same window drives both the prefetch and the look-ahead LRU updates.
result.corrections:
The core claim holds: SSD->DRAM prefetch for waiting-queue requests inside a look-ahead window, plus a look-ahead LRU that uses pending requests to protect their chunks from eviction. The nuances below matter.

(a) "Fixed 4-request window" is too strong. 4 is the default in the implementation ("set to 4 in our configuration"). It is a tunable, static hyperparameter, not a design constant. The ablation finds window 6 best for Llama2-7B (31.06% lower TTFT than 4 at high request rate), and the authors recommend profiling per model. The window is static in the sense that it does not adapt to load or queue time. However, Algorithm 1 has unexplained "EnforcePrefetchWindow"/"ShrinkPrefetchWindow" steps, and the window slides forward each cycle.

(b) The "look-ahead LRU" uses the same preloading window, not just the next request, although the 4.2 example looks only at "the next request". Its protection is a recency/priority bump inside LRU ordering ("update the recency for matched chunks", "increases the priority"), not a guaranteed pin.

(c) It applies to the CPU-DRAM/SSD chunk tiers managed by PCR's own prefix tree. GPU KV is left to vLLM, so the look-ahead does not protect GPU-resident prefix cache.

(d) Context: the paper targets RAG serving and is built on vLLM. It is an arXiv v1 preprint with no confirmed peer-reviewed venue.
quotes: "(1) a prefix-tree caching structure with a look-ahead LRU replacement policy that uses pending requests in the scheduler queue to improve cache hit ratios; (2) layer-wise overlapping that pipelines KV-cache loading and GPU computation across CUDA streams to hide communication latency; and (3) queue-based prefetching that proactively loads relevant KV caches from SSD into DRAM before they are needed." (Abstract)

"To further improve the cache hit ratio, we introduce a look-ahead update mechanism that leverages pending requests from the waiting queue to predict near-future reuse and protect corresponding chunks from eviction. For instance, when one chunk must be evicted to insert a new chunk C9, a look-ahead to the next request increases the priority of C2 (the oldest chunk). Consequently, instead of evicting C2, the algorithm removes the second-oldest leaf, C4" (Sec. 4.2)

"Because each chunk depends on its parent node and can only be reused when its parent also resides in the cache, eviction is restricted to the leaf nodes of the tree. As illustrated in the figure, all leaves are maintained using an LRU (Least Recently Used) cache replacement policy" (Sec. 4.2)

"the prefetcher maintains a look-ahead window to identify requests within a certain range of the queue. It then checks the KV-cache status of these requests in both DRAM and SSD. If a KV cache is found on the SSD but not yet in DRAM, the prefetcher launches asynchronous loading tasks to transfer it into DRAM." (Sec. 4.4)
"After each prefetching cycle, the look-ahead window slides forward to track subsequent requests." (Sec. 4.4)

"This observation implies that requests in the waiting queue have already completed their document retrieval phase, creating an opportunity to prefetch their KV caches from SSD into DRAM before computation begins." (Sec. 4.4)

"For queue-based prefetching and look-ahead LRU cache policy, we monitor the request waiting queue within the vLLM scheduler. We send the waiting requests within a preloading window (set to 4 in our configuration) to the cache engine of PCR, and update the recency for matched chunks and use a dedicated thread (e.g., Prefetcher) to fetch the KV cache from SSD to CPU memory upon prefix matching." (Sec. 5)
"6: if in CPU cache then BumpPriority ( key ) 7: else if in SSD cache then SubmitSSDToCPULoad ( key ) 8: else break ... EnforcePrefetchWindow ... ShrinkPrefetchWindow" (Algorithm 1 PCR_step)

"we split sequences into chunks and manage their KV cache chunks in CPU memory and SSD by constructing a prefix tree structure, leaving GPU memory management to vLLM. For efficient management and movement, our chunk size is typically larger than the block size of vLLM (256 vs. 16 in the our setting)." (Sec. 5)

"The TTFT is reduced by 31.06% when the window size is changed from 4 to 6 for high request rate. ... the results indicate that a window size of 6 is optimal for both high and low request rates for Llama2-7B in our environment. However, different models may require different optimal window sizes, so we recommend profiling the performance to identify the best configuration for each model." (Sec. 6.4)

result.date_or_venue: 2024 USENIX Annual Technical Conference (USENIX ATC '24), July 10–12, 2024, Santa Clara, CA, pp. 111–126. Authors: Bin Gao, Zhuomin He, Puru Sharma, Qingxuan Kang, Djordje Jevdjic, Junbo Deng, Xingkun Yang, Zhou Yu, Pengfei Zuo. Also arXiv:2403.19708 (v1 2024-03-23, v3 2024-06-30, "Accepted to USENIX Annual Technical Conference (ATC) 2024"). An earlier arXiv version used the name "AttentionStore"; in the ATC version AttentionStore is the hierarchical KV store inside CachedAttention.
result.url_checked: https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.19708 ; https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.19708v3 (full text extracted) ; https://www.usenix.org/system/files/atc24-gao-bin-cost.pdf (ATC camera-ready, same §3.3 text) ; https://www.usenix.org/conference/atc24/presentation/gao-bin-cost
result.what_it_actually_does:
AttentionStore is the tiered KV store in CachedAttention: HBM for execution and read/write buffers, host DRAM, and SSD disks. KV placement between DRAM and disk is decided only by the position of *already-queued* jobs in the inference job scheduler's queue. It does not use time, predicted arrival, or reuse-distance estimates.

(1) Scheduler-aware fetching (§3.3.1, disk→DRAM): a look-ahead prefetching window covers the waiting jobs at the head of the queue. For each job in that window whose session KV is on disk, fetching threads copy it to DRAM before the job runs. Window length Lpw = Cmem/Skv, where Cmem is the DRAM capacity available for prefetching and Skv is the average per-session KV size. The window is therefore counted in jobs; Figure 9 uses size 2, covering Jobs 2–3 while Job 1 runs. A DRAM buffer is kept free: when free memory drops to a threshold, a DRAM→disk eviction starts.

(2) Scheduler-aware eviction (§3.3.2): a look-ahead eviction window in the job queue, length (Cmem+Cdisk)/Skv, i.e. the whole store's capacity counted in sessions.
- When evicting an item out of AttentionStore entirely (disk full), an item inside the eviction window is exempted. In the example, the last-arrived Job 9, which is outside the window, is dropped.
- When evicting from DRAM to disk, the item at the tail of the eviction window has higher priority. The example first checks for DRAM entries with no queued job, then scans the window from tail to head. It evicts Job 4, which is inside the window.

(3) Granularity: one item is all the KV of a conversation session. That is the minimum unit for both fetching and eviction ("either all used or none of it is used").

(4) Separately (§3.2.1), DRAM→HBM layer-wise pre-loading overlaps KV loading with prefill. An HBM read buffer lets loading for the next job start while the previous job is still running. The buffer is sized Sbuf = B(Tload·Lhist − Tpref·Lnew).

Evaluation (§4.3.3): with 128G DRAM / 10T SSD, overall hit rate is 86%, against 58% for LRU and 48% for FIFO, and over 99.6% of hits are in DRAM.
result.corrections:
All the claim's core points check out against the primary text: the look-ahead prefetching window, Lpw = Cmem/Skv, prefetching only from disk to host memory, windows counted in jobs, whole-session items, exemption within the eviction window, and tail-first eviction. Four refinements:
(a) The paper states the exemption rule only for evicting an item out of AttentionStore entirely, i.e. dropping it from disk. For DRAM→disk eviction, items inside the window are not exempt; the one nearest the tail of the window is evicted first. In the Figure 9 example, Job 4 is inside the size-6 window and is still moved to disk. Saying "exempts jobs in the window and evicts from the tail" merges two tier-specific rules.
(b) The eviction window length is (Cmem+Cdisk)/Skv, the whole store's capacity, not Cmem/Skv. The paper calls this the "maximum length".
(c) Skv is the average KV size per session, so the job-count windows are capacity divided by an average session size, not an exact per-job count.
(d) The windows only cover jobs already waiting in the scheduler queue. There is no prediction of future turns that have not arrived yet and no time-based signal. Prefetch lead time is bounded by how long a job waits in the queue.
quotes: "CachedAttention applies a look-ahead prefetching window to watch for the waiting jobs to be executed. If the KV cache of the waiting jobs is hit in the disks, CachedAttention will pre-fetch the KV cache of waiting jobs from the disks to host memory before these waiting jobs are executed." (§3.3.1)

"The length of the look-ahead prefetching window is determined by the available capacity in the host memory. Given the available memory capacity for prefetching Cmem and the average KV size of a session Skv, the prefetching window length is Lpw = Cmem/Skv." (§3.3.1)

"As Job 1 is executing, the KV cache manager applies a look-ahead window size of 2 (the host memory has 2 KV cache slots for the KV cache fetching) to check the KV cache hit status of the waiting Jobs 2-3." (§3.3.1)

"When the capacity of the free memory reaches a defined threshold, CachedAttention triggers a KV eviction from host memory to disks to ensure the constant availability of the host memory buffer." (§3.3.1)

"CachedAttention maintains a look-ahead eviction window in the job queue. The maximum length of the look-ahead eviction window is determined by the total storage capacity of AttentionStore. Assume the total available capacity in the disks is Cdisk. The look-ahead eviction window length is (Cmem + Cdisk)/Skv." (§3.3.2)

"When CachedAttention attempts to evict one item out of AttentionStore, if finding the item to be evicted in the look-ahead eviction window, the item is exempted. When CachedAttention evicts one item from the host memory to disks, the item located at the tail of the look-ahead eviction window has a higher priority to be evicted." (§3.3.2)

"Note that one item corresponds to all KV caches associated with a conversation session, which is the minimal eviction and fetching granularity in CachedAttention. This is because the KV cache in the same conversation session is either all used or none of it is used." (§3.3.2)

"First, it finds that the KV caches in the host memory all have an associated job in the job queue. It then proceeds to scan the look-ahead eviction window from tail to head, prioritizing the eviction of jobs near the tail. Therefore, the KV cache for Job 4 is selected to be evicted from the host memory to the disks. Since the disks are also full, the scanning process identifies that the last arrived Job 9 in the job queue is the most suitable candidate to be evicted." (§3.3.2)
"Figure 9: Scheduler-aware KV cache fetching and eviction." [figure labels: "eviction window, size: 6", "prefetching window, size: 2"]
"The read stream can start the pre-loading while the last job is running." (§3.2.1, DRAM->HBM layer-wise pre-loading with HBM read buffer)
"CA achieves a cache hit rate of up to 86%, with over 99.6% of the hits occurring in DRAM due to its scheduler-aware policy." (§4.3.3)

result.exact_title: Continuum: Efficient and Robust Multi-Turn LLM Agent Scheduling with KV Cache Time-to-Live
result.date_or_venue: arXiv preprint 2511.02230 [cs.OS]. v1 submitted 2025-11-04; later versions v2 (2025-12-20), v3 (2026-01-30), v4 (2026-05-04), v5 (2026-05-11), v6 (2026-05-25), v7 (2026-09-08, current). No peer-reviewed venue is listed on the abs page. Authors: Hanchen Li, Runyuan He, Qiuyang Mang, Qizheng Zhang, Huanzhi Mao, Xiaokun Chen, Hangrui Zhou, Huanchen Zhang, Alvin Cheung, Joseph Gonzalez, Ion Stoica (UC Berkeley et al.). Built on vLLM 0.10.2 (plus LMCache for CPU/SSD offload baselines).
result.url_checked: https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.02230 ; https://arxiv.org/html/2511.02230 (v7) ; https://arxiv.org/html/2511.02230v1 ; https://arxiv.org/html/2511.02230v2 ; v3 ; v4
result.what_it_actually_does:
When a request's output contains a tool call, Continuum decides how long to pin that request's KV cache in GPU memory (a TTL) instead of evicting it when the turn ends. In the current version (v2 onward, including v7), it picks τ* = argmax_τ P(τ,f)·(T·η + Prefill-Reload(r)) − τ. The terms are:
- P(τ,f) is the empirical CDF of past durations for the same tool f (S[f]). A duration is measured as the gap between one request finishing and the next request of the same program_id arriving.
- T is a sliding-window average of the queueing delay seen by requests that were evicted.
- η = −Corr(k, N−k) is a "memoryfulness" factor for the workload.
- Prefill-Reload(r) is the cost to recompute or reload the prefix, taken from offline profiling (a prefill-vs-context-length curve, plus GPU-CPU bandwidth when CPU offload is on).

To solve it, the system tries every recorded duration in S[f] (and τ=0) as a candidate. It falls back when data is thin: first to the global CDF over all tools, then to a fixed T_default. T_default comes from assuming Exp(1) tool durations and η=1.

When the TTL expires, the KV is unpinned and becomes evictable from GPU. It is not unpinned while the program's next request is already in the waiting queue. It is also unpinned early when the program ends, or to break a deadlock (the pin whose program arrived latest goes first). The pinning works together with program-level FCFS priority.

Tiers: the decision is about keeping KV in GPU HBM. CPU DRAM and SSD offload (LMCache) enter only through the reload-cost term and the evaluation baselines. Reload on the next turn is reactive. The paper has no prefetch or proactive-reload mechanism: the word "prefetch" does not appear in v7. So "retention TTL, not fetch timing" is correct.
result.corrections:
The claim is accurate for v2 through v7, but it has four gaps.

1. **Version.** The CDF plus sliding-window design is not in v1 (2025-11-04). v1 used per-tool and global mean/variance statistics (μ̂_f, σ̂_f) to get an upper bound B_f(δ) at confidence 1−δ. It scaled the TTL by average turn count (AvgTurns) and had no queueing-delay estimate. Cite v2 or later (such as v7) when describing the CDF plus sliding-window mechanism.

2. **Missing terms.** The objective also includes the prefill/reload cost Prefill-Reload(r) and the memoryfulness factor η. The sliding-window queueing delay is multiplied by η.

3. **Fallbacks.** The per-tool CDF falls back to a global CDF and then to a fixed T_default.

4. **Duration measurement.** A tool's duration is the inter-request interval within a program_id. It is not a direct timing of the tool.

Also note that the paper body (v7 HTML and the abstract) often misspells the system as "Continnum". The official title metadata reads "Continuum".
quotes: Title metadata (abs page): "Continuum: Efficient and Robust Multi-Turn LLM Agent Scheduling with KV Cache Time-to-Live"; citation_date "2025/11/04"; HTML header: "arXiv:2511.02230v7 [cs.OS] 08 Sep 2026"

Abstract: "For requests that generate tool calls, Continnum selectively pins the KV cache in GPU memory with a time-to-live value determined by the reload cost and potential queueing delay induced by eviction. When the TTL expires, the KV cache can be automatically evicted to free up GPU memory, providing robust performance under edge cases."
v7 Eq. (2): "argmax τ 𝒫(τ,f) × (𝒯 ⋅ η + Prefill-Reload(r)) − τ, indicating that we only need to additionally compute 𝒯 and 𝒫(τ,f) in our implementation."

v7: "𝒯 can be estimated as the sliding window average for queueing delay experienced by requests who was evicted. Since we cannot fully predict the duration of the next tool call, we estimate 𝒫(τ,f) using the empirical CDF derived from historical tool-call records S[f]."

v7: "𝒫(τ,f) = 1/|S[f]| ⋅ ∑_{t∈S[f]} 𝕀[t ≤ τ] ... Finally, we solve Equation (2) by enumerating all unique tool-call durations recorded in S[f] as candidates (including τ = 0) and selecting the one with the highest expected reward."
v7: "We define the following memoryfulness factor η = − Corr(k, N − k)"
v7: "Prefill-Reload(r) is the time cost for prefill or reloading depending on whether CPU offloading is turned on. This is based on a quick offline profiling described in Sec 5.2."

v7 cold start: "we first try to use the global tool-call information to estimate 𝒫(τ,f_any) ... we design a minimal version of Continnum that uses a fixed TTL threshold T_default, derived from the same cost model by assuming that the tool-call duration follows an exponential distribution with unit mean"

v7: "The handler parses tool calls from LLM outputs, tracks per-tool latency using observed inter-request intervals within the same program_id, and returns TTL to the scheduler. The scheduler uses this hint to pin the request's KV cache for potential reuse by the next step, and later unpins it either when the TTL value expires or when the program terminates."

v7: "If the KV cache was evicted for this step, the engine must recompute the prefix (prefill) or reload from CPU (if CPU offloading is enabled) when the tool execution completes and the next inference step begins."
v7: "We implemented Continnum on top of vLLM with about 1k lines of Python."

v1 (older mechanism): "we set the timeout based on the predicted upper bounds B(δ) and B_f(δ) of the tool-call intervals, with a confidence level of 1 − δ ... Concretely, we scale the TTL by the average number of turns, AvgTurns, across all programs"

result.what_it_actually_does:
The failure mode is described accurately. Native vLLM tiered offload uses TieringOffloadingManager with a filesystem secondary tier. It starts a disk->CPU promotion on every scheduler lookup() that finds the prefix on disk, including lookups for waiting requests that the scheduler then skips. With many queued long-context requests, several promotions reserve most of the CPU pool at the same time. Stores can then fail to get staging memory, and a promotion can be evicted as soon as it lands, before its request reads it. The paper says the request's later demand load "may" find no free CPU memory and "fall back to recomputing the prefix". The evicted data is also re-promoted from disk again and again: the paper measured 3.4 TB read from disk by native vLLM against 85 GB for py-kvcache, and only two requests ever moved promoted data from CPU to GPU.

The "remedy" in the claim combines two separate fixes from different authors:

(1) py-kvcache, the paper's own vLLM KV Offload connector. It uses scheduler-aware preloading. A bounded on_preload_candidates callback examines "a bounded lookahead of waiting requests" and sends preload plans only when the storage path has capacity. Preloaded blocks land in a bounded shared CPU staging pool, and the later demand load claims them. It allows only one speculative preload at a time. Preloads give way to demand loads: they stop issuing, or an open speculative read is closed and requeued. Memory reserved per load or store is capped at the configured I/O depth, which in the paper's configuration means 576 MB of free CPU memory. The paper does NOT describe protecting or pinning unread promotions. Its lesson is that speculative work must be bounded and must yield to demand.

result.what_it_actually_does:
The paper does not predict tool duration from history. Its signal is live progress that the tool reports while it runs. A two-layer harness reads the tool's byte stream (verbose flags, dry-run totals) and its environment (for example object files appearing on disk). It sends these as timestamped progress events through a side channel, so what the agent sees does not change. Each progress report is converted linearly into an estimate of remaining time. A controller runs beside the harness.

- **GPU memory only (HBM):** the controller keeps (refreshes) a context while the reported remaining time is under a keep threshold. Once the estimate moves well past the threshold, it stops refreshing and the context ages out under LRU.
- **With a host tier (HBM + DRAM):** the controller adds hysteresis, releasing a context only once the estimate is well past the threshold. It also "refreshes the context one lead time before the predicted return and reloads it if it has gone."
- **Engine patch:** the engine is vLLM with prefix caching, and the host tier is vLLM's own KV offload to DRAM. The patch adds a route with three operations. Refresh moves resident blocks to the safe end of the eviction queue at no cost, which is an LRU bump, not by itself a copy from DRAM to HBM. Release moves blocks to the front of that queue while keeping them addressable. Query reports how much of a context is resident. The scheduler and its eviction rule are unchanged.
- **Lead time:** the paper frames timing as a "recovery budget", defined as the time it takes to get a context back. The accuracy analysis uses two settings, 2 s and 0.5 s. No queueing, scheduler-wait or contention term appears in the controller or in the lead time. The only "queue" in the text is the engine's eviction queue.
- **Evaluation data:**
  - Replays of agent sessions: mini-SWE-agent SWE-bench leaderboard runs (six submissions, about 3,000 trajectories), OpenHands evaluation runs, and the authors' own runs on 100 SWE-bench Verified tasks with Qwen 3.8 Flash.
  - The census also covers Terminal-Bench and OpenTelemetry traces.
  - The end-to-end runs are on 4×H100 SXM in two settings: GPU memory only, and GPU memory plus DRAM. There is no SSD or disk KV tier.
- **Baselines:** Continuum, CacheWise, TokenCake and InferCept, reimplemented, plus LRU and an oracle.
- **Results:** p90 TTFT after a tool call falls by 20.7% (HBM only) and 20.8% (HBM + DRAM) against LRU. CacheWise, TokenCake and InferCept keep nearly everything. In the DRAM setting they cut p90 TTFT by 15–18%, but they reload 8–13× the proposed method's volume from DRAM.
result.corrections:
The core claim is right: one lead time before the predicted return, HBM/DRAM only, and no queue term. Several details are loose or leave out conditions:

1. **Refresh vs. reload.** In the paper, "refresh" is an LRU bump of blocks already resident in the engine. The copy from DRAM to HBM is the separate "reloads it if it has gone" step. Both happen one lead time before the predicted return. The "predicted return" comes from the tool's live progress stream, not from a history-based model. That run-time signal is the paper's key novelty and should be named.
2. **"~80% off" holds only near the end of a call.** The 80% median error, relative to the call's duration, is for the best history predictor at 90% of each call. The progress stream's error there is under 10%. At 50% of the call, the best history predictor's error is about a third, against about a fifth for the progress stream. The median error is not 80% overall.
3. **8–13× reload volume.** This applies only in the HBM + DRAM setting and only to CacheWise, TokenCake and InferCept. It is measured against the paper's own method, not against LRU. Continuum falls back to LRU instead. Those three predictors still cut p90 TTFT by 15–18% against LRU.
4. **"SWE-agent replays" is too narrow.** The replays combine mini-SWE-agent leaderboard runs on SWE-bench, OpenHands evaluation runs, and the authors' own runs on SWE-bench Verified. The census adds Terminal-Bench and OpenTelemetry traces.
5. **Missing context.** The system is built on vLLM, not SGLang, using a patch of a few hundred lines on 4×H100 SXM.
6. **"No queue term" rests on absence from the text.** No queueing or scheduler-wait term appears in the controller description (Sec 5.1, App. D). The lead time is described only as the time it takes to get a context back.

result.what_it_actually_does:
2608.30830 (Adaptive KV Retention): this paper is about requests that pause for minutes to hours while waiting for human approval, not seconds-scale tool calls. Tiers are HBM, host DRAM and discard-then-recompute. Each tier is costed as C_j(l) = alpha_j*l + beta_j, measured in GPU time. HBM has a holding cost alpha1. A DRAM copy costs beta2 to restore. Discarding costs beta3 to recompute.

Suspended KV is always offloaded HBM to DRAM at suspension, because the break-even point t1 is about 1 s. The only remaining decision is how long to keep the DRAM copy. Little's law (N = lambda*W) sets the point where the host tier saturates: lambda_crit = C2/W_ref. C2 is how many suspended contexts fit in host memory, and W_ref is a 1,800 s reference wait. Above lambda_crit, a mean-field congestion price alpha2(lambda) = max(0, lambda - lambda_crit)*beta3/C2 gives the DRAM TTL. It is t2(lambda) = infinity when lambda <= lambda_crit, and (beta3 - beta2)/alpha2(lambda) otherwise. This policy is called cpu_ttl(lambda).

Before serving, the controller replays a separate sample of calibration waits under both modes. It then picks either host-retain (keep the copy until resume) or cpu_ttl(lambda), whichever costs less, and freezes that choice. At runtime its only input is the offered load lambda. In the experiments this is the configured offered rate, not a live measurement. The TTL is set once and never re-scored as the wait goes on. The live host tier evicts in this order: expired blocks, then transient blocks of active requests, then LRU suspended blocks. Prefetch or promotion before resume does not appear (the full text has zero matches for "prefetch"). The paper treats resume latency as secondary at these timescales. Tested with Llama-3.1-70B TP4 on 4x H100 NVL with vLLM, a 375-380 GB host budget, and replay at multiples of lambda_crit.

2609.16215 (Where Should the KV Cache Live?): this is a discrete-event simulator of GPU HBM, CPU DRAM and SSD, calibrated against a random-forest execution-time predictor. It runs at batch size one on one GPU, with synthetic chat, agent and document-QA workloads. The paper compares recency, reuse-frequency, predicted-reuse and EWMA placement policies. It tests prefetch with three arms (none, a causal predictor, a future-reading oracle) on a "bandwidth-charged model" where speculative fetches compete with demand fetches on the same link. The oracle is always judged against no-prefetch. The abstract states the metric as migration traffic, and the body talks about stalls, being "slower". The result is negative: the causal predictor gets a positive share of the oracle's gain in no cell, and the oracle beats no-prefetch in no cell. The stated reason is that on a contended link a speculative fetch delays the demand fetch a request is waiting on.
result.corrections:
Both papers exist with the cited IDs, and both claims match what the papers say. The caveats below should go with the citation.

(1) 2608.30830: Little's law does not set the residency time directly. It only sets the saturation threshold lambda_crit = C2/W_ref. The TTL itself comes from a mean-field congestion price: t2 = (beta3 - beta2)/alpha2(lambda). Below lambda_crit, retention is indefinite. The choice between indefinite retention and the load-indexed TTL is made offline from calibration samples and then frozen. Lambda is the configured offered rate, not a measured one. The paper covers retention and expiry only, with no prefetch or reload timing. It is also scoped to minute-to-hour human-approval waits, where it calls resume latency secondary.

(2) 2609.16215: this is a simulation-only result at batch size one on a single GPU, with synthetic workloads. In this setup, fetch stall is under 1% of TPOT. The authors say the result "does not contradict systems where prefetch helps, since those overlap transfer with abundant spare bandwidth". They also say the value of prefetch "would rise" at larger batch sizes. The prefetch tested is generic block lookahead ("++ prefetch" as a roadmap recommended it), not prefetch timed to a known resume or tool-return event.

The paper is also not fully consistent. The abstract says the oracle "never beats no prefetch on migration traffic". Section V-E says the oracle "is slower than not prefetching in over half of" the cells, which implies ties elsewhere, not losses everywhere. The paper is a cs.AI preprint that has not been peer-reviewed. Anyone citing it should say that "does not pay on a contended link" applies to this simulator's setup, where bandwidth is already scarce.

result.what_it_actually_does:
KVFlow (accurate): the agent schedule is modelled as an Agent Step Graph. Each agent gets a steps-to-execution value, which sets eviction priority per radix-tree KV node. CPU memory acts as a second-tier cache for the fixed-prompt KV of evicted agents. While the current agent runs, background threads proactively prefetch CPU->GPU the KV of agents scheduled in the next step. When the graph branches, it prefetches every possible next agent, up to a cap on concurrent prefetches. Status-aware scheduling skips requests whose nodes are still loading, using the node states GPU / CPU backup / loading / offloading. Signal: the frontend passes workflow step information to the server. Prototype built on SGLang v0.4.4 and compared against SGLang's hierarchical radix cache.

SAGA (timing accurate, tier wrong): it is built on vLLM v0.6.0 and keeps KV in GPU HBM. When an Agent Execution Graph node finishes inference and starts tool execution, SAGA picks the most likely successor and starts prefetching that successor's prefix KV into spare GPU memory on separate CUDA streams, overlapping the tool call. The paper does not say where the prefetched KV comes from. It explicitly turns down host-DRAM offload/swap during tool gaps ("We chose HBM retention with predictive eviction") and calls a host-DRAM third tier future work. So "prefetch at tool start" is correct, but SAGA is not CPU->GPU. Other mechanisms: WA-LRU workflow-aware eviction and a tool-call-aware TTL (the p-th percentile of a per-tool-type log-normal latency fit, scaled down under memory pressure).

PBKV (mostly accurate, with nuances): built on SGLang with two tiers, a GPU Radix Tree and a HiCache host-memory tier. A learned predictor (GraphSAGE over a global call graph, plus attention over the workflow prefix, plus the prefill hidden state) forecasts the next K agent invocations for each workflow. Eviction is hierarchical: retired cache from finished workflows goes first, then active cache ranked by a K-step lookahead reuse score aggregated across workflows. Prefetch moves host->GPU (CPU->GPU over PCIe) the cache nodes likely to be reused "before they are hit". Candidates are ranked by the one-step reuse value (Eq. 1), which comes from the predicted next-agent probability distribution. Prefetch runs only on pure-decode batches. Its budget is the smaller of (free space + retired cache) and (PCIe bandwidth x decode-step time), filled greedily, and it never evicts active cache.
result.corrections: 1) The blanket "all CPU->GPU" is wrong for SAGA. SAGA prefetches into spare GPU memory, rejects host-DRAM swap, and calls a host-DRAM tier future work. Its prefetch source tier is unspecified. SAGA is also built on vLLM, not SGLang. It should be described as "HBM-retention + speculative prefetch of the likely successor's prefix KV at tool start, source tier unspecified". 2) PBKV is not "keyed on workflow step" in a deterministic sense. It ranks host-tier nodes by a learned predictor's one-step next-agent probability (the reuse value, Eq. 1) and targets dynamic workflows. PBKV itself says KVFlow's steps-to-execution distance "is undefined under runtime-dependent loops". Its prefetch timing is opportunistic: it fires on pure-decode batches, within a free-space + retired-cache and PCIe budget, before the cache is hit. It is not a fixed trigger tied to request arrival. Calling it "pre-arrival" is fair only loosely, as "before they are hit". 3) KVFlow is described accurately: NeurIPS 2025, SGLang v0.4.4, Agent Step Graph / steps-to-execution drive eviction, and proactive CPU->GPU prefetch of the next-step agents. A small addition: it also has status-aware scheduling, and it prefetches all possible next agents when the graph branches, up to a limit.

result.what_it_actually_does:
Paper (v4; v1 describes the same mechanism):
- Temporal Scheduler. It is event-driven. A call_start event (the agent emits a function call) runs an opportunistic gate that decides whether to offload that agent's KV from GPU to CPU asynchronously. The gate predicts a function-call (FC) duration T_fc and rejects the offload if T_fc <= T_transfer, where T_transfer is the round-trip offload+upload time, linear in block count and calibrated from measured per-block constants. It then turns T_window = T_fc - T_transfer into a token capacity using observed decode throughput, and first-fit searches the waiting queue for a request that fits the freed blocks. There are four hard rejections: CPU capacity too low, stall too short, no waiting request fits, or GPU pressure below a watermark. A soft score follows; it penalizes critical-path agents, near-completion requests and high migration churn, with an emergency override. So offload during a function call is conditional, not automatic.
- Prediction. It is per function type. With no history it uses the user's predict_time from the graph (DAG) API, or a conservative constant. After the first observation it uses an EWMA, blended with the user estimate as t_estimate = α·t_user + (1−α)·t_history. The observed time is fed back.
- Predictive upload. "As the predicted completion time approaches", the scheduler starts a gradual upload. In practice the gradual part is GPU destination-block reservation: at most ceil(deficit/2) per scheduling step, capped by an upload budget that protects critical waiting requests (B_upload = max(0, B_gpu_free − max(0, D_critical − B_shared_free))). Candidates are ranked by P_upload = I + U, where I is importance from the Spatial Scheduler's priority metric and U is urgency from proximity to the predicted FC completion. If the tool returns early, the upload starts immediately.
- Tiers. GPU and a CPU block pool only. No SSD or disk tier. Evaluation is single-GPU. A neighbouring GPU over NVLink is mentioned only as future work.
- Queue wait. Upload timing and urgency depend only on predicted FC completion. The resumed request's post-return queueing delay is not modelled. Queue wait time does appear elsewhere: in the Spatial Scheduler's per-request priority P_req, inside the aging term f_aging.
- Implementation. About 9k lines of Python reusing vLLM (paper baselines on vLLM v0.8.6).

Released code (pku-lemonade/TokenCake, ported to vLLM v0.22.0):
- The README says the implementation does "event-driven preservation with demand-triggered CPU-to-GPU recovery" and that predictive prefetching is still in development.
- lifecycle.py keeps an EWMA (ewma_alpha=0.5) keyed by (agent_type or agent_name, event kind), not strictly by tool. It averages this 0.5/0.5 with the caller's estimated_duration_s, defaulting to default_stall_s=1.0.
- The prediction is used to size the preservation window and to set a CPU "ownership release" deadline. It does not trigger a prefetch.
- Restore goes through vLLM's native OffloadingConnector prefix lookup when the request is scheduled again.
result.corrections:
No part of the claim is wrong, but several details need precision.
(1) "Per-tool EWMA": the paper says "per-function-type". The EWMA is used only after the first observation and is blended with the user-supplied predict_time (α·t_user + (1−α)·t_history). In the released code the key is agent_type/agent_name plus event kind, not a tool name.
(2) "Offloads KV to CPU during function calls": this happens only when an opportunistic, multi-condition gate approves it. The stall must exceed the round-trip transfer, a waiting request must fit the freed blocks, CPU capacity and a GPU-pressure watermark must be met, and a soft score must pass. It is not done for every call.
(3) "Gradual upload": the gradual part is GPU destination-block reservation (at most half of the remaining deficit per step), ranked by P_upload = I + U. An early tool return triggers an immediate upload.
(4) "No queue-wait term": true for upload timing and urgency, since U depends only on proximity to the predicted FC completion. However, the paper's per-request priority P_req has an aging term that includes "queue wait time", and upload ranking reuses the Spatial Scheduler's "importance" (I). So a queue-wait signal may enter the upload ordering indirectly, though never the start time.
(5) "GPU/CPU only": correct. NVLink-to-a-neighbouring-GPU is mentioned only as future work.
(6) "Released code demand-triggered": correct and stated verbatim in the repo README (vLLM v0.22.0 port, repo created 2026-09-15). The code's prediction sets a CPU ownership release deadline, not a prefetch.
(7) EuroSys '27: supported by the arXiv comments field ("Accepted at EuroSys '27") and the repo badge. I did not check the EuroSys program itself. The artifact evaluation repo names the paper "SunCake".

Abstract: "TokenCake's Temporal Scheduler employs an event-driven, opportunistic policy to proactively offload idle KV Caches during function calls and uses predictive uploading to hide data transfer latency."

§4.1: "A call_start event fires when an agent emits a function call. The scheduler consults the opportunistic policy (§ 4.2 ) to decide whether offloading the agent's KV Cache is worthwhile. If the policy approves, the KV Cache is transferred to CPU memory asynchronously. As the predicted completion time approaches, the scheduler begins a gradual upload (§ 4.3 ) to hide transfer latency behind other computation."

§4.1: "If the tool returns earlier than predicted, the scheduler triggers an immediate upload to ensure correctness. The observed execution time is fed back to the forecasting model to refine future predictions."

§4.1 Dynamic Forecasting: "The scheduler maintains a per-function-type time estimate. When no history is available, the estimate defaults to the value supplied by the user through the graph definition, or to a conservative system-wide constant if no user estimate exists. §4.2: "Offloading is beneficial only when three conditions hold simultaneously: the predicted stall is long enough to cover a round-trip transfer, a waiting request exists that can use the freed GPU blocks, and the later upload can be prepared without displacing more important work."

§4.2: "Before computing any score, the policy applies four hard rejections: CPU capacity is insufficient, the predicted stall is shorter than the transfer time, no waiting request fits within the freed blocks, or GPU memory pressure is below a configurable threshold."

result.what_it_actually_does:
#39283 (merged) adds Scheduler._prefetch_after_device_hit_loss. The function is present at merge commit 7f5dd19 and on current main, around line 3212 of scheduler.py. How it works:
- _prefetch_kvcache records req.storage_prefetch_last_match_len = len(prefix_indices) + host_hit_length each time it plans an L3 lookup, which happens at arrival and again on every re-issue.
- In the waiting-queue admission loop, right after req.init_next_round_input, the function recomputes the current device+host match. If that match is shorter than the recorded length, it logs "device prefix shrank before admission", calls _retry_storage_prefetch (which re-issues the L3 query and increments storage_prefetch_retry_attempts) and returns True. The loop then `continue`s, so the request is skipped on that pass.
- It does nothing when there was no earlier lookup, or when the buffer pipeline already holds a staged prefetch for the request.
- It is capped by --hicache-storage-prefetch-retry-max-attempts (default 8). Past the cap, the shorter live match is accepted and the request is admitted as is.
So it is reactive. It detects the loss at admission time and does not protect the prefix while the request waits in the queue.

The same PR also:
- moves retries into StoragePrefetchRetries: paced miss polls, immediate re-issues for known hits whose anchor moved, and the per-request cap;
- adds a FULL-only pin (match_full_device_prefix, inc_full_pin, dec_full_pin) that stops the device prefix under a staged or parked buffer-mode fetch from being evicted;
- bounds staged-admission deferrals (max_staged_admission_defers = 32).

#40042 (merged) does not add the function. It is a one-line change in UnifiedRadixCache.prefetch_from_storage: a too-short or fully-device-matched decline no longer calls storage_prefetch_retries.poll_miss. This stops no-op polls from using up the re-issue budget, so the admission-time device-hit-loss re-query always has budget left.

#40011 is the same change opened by a bot. It was closed unmerged in favour of #40042. Its description contains the quoted phrase word for word.

#31887 (a draft, closed, never merged) proposes:
- durable per-request prefetch states, waiting-queue retries and bounded admission deadlines;
- checkpoint fields and handles for RL rollouts;
- an opt-in, physically isolated L3 staging partition (SGLANG_HICACHE_L3_STAGING_RESERVE_RATIO).

#32724 is an issue, not a PR. It reports that a storage prefetch is only finalized (check_prefetch_progress: host radix insertion, host memory release, ongoing_prefetch cleanup) when the FCFS waiting-queue scan reaches the request. It proposes finalizing early at check_hicache_events. The fix is PR #32725, which is still open.

RFC #27574 lists Prefetch in its hint taxonomy. Its roadmap defers it with "TODO - measure request-time L3 restoration before adding proactive Prefetch or Demote execution APIs".

RFC #36224 defines kv.prefetch@1.0 only as restoring storage for the current request. It lists proactive pre-arrival transfer as a non-goal.

result.what_it_actually_does: FORESTALL (Kimbrel et al., OSDI'96): a new hybrid of fixed horizon (TIP), aggressive (Cao et al.) and reverse aggressive. The setting is a single process that gives full hints, with parallel disks. Let d_i be the distance from the cursor to the i-th missing block and F the ratio of fetch time to per-reference compute time. Forestall starts a prefetch (choosing the next missing block to fetch and evicting the block whose next use is furthest away) when i*F >= d_i holds for some i, and only if the Do-No-Harm rule allows it. So it prefetches just early enough to avoid a stall. When several missing blocks are bunched together in the hinted future (heavy upcoming disk load, i.e. I/O-bound), the test fires early and it acts like aggressive. When misses are sparse (compute-bound), it waits like fixed horizon and makes late, better eviction choices. Practical details: F is estimated per disk as the ratio of the sum of the last 100 disk access times to the sum of the last 100 inter-reference CPU times. An overestimate F' is used, set from the observed average disk access time. The test only checks missing blocks within K (the cache size) of the cursor. Because the CSCAN disk scheduler reorders requests, fixed horizon's rule of fetching any missing block within H of the cursor was also added. Requests are batched. The signal is a prediction of upcoming disk load, made from the hinted reference string plus measured fetch and compute times. It is not an observed queue depth. The setting is one cache over d disks, not a multi-tier hierarchy. CAO et al. (SIGMETRICS'95): four rules that an optimal integrated prefetching and caching policy must follow: Rule 1 Optimal Prefetching, Rule 2 Optimal Replacement, Rule 3 Do No Harm and Rule 4 First Opportunity. The model is a single disk. The paper also defines the Conservative strategy (MIN's replacements, each fetch at the earliest opportunity; at most 2x optimal) and the Aggressive strategy (always fetch the next missing block at the earliest opportunity allowed by the rules). TIP (Patterson et al., SOSP'95): application hints drive prefetching, and cost-benefit analysis divides buffers among prefetching, caching hinted blocks, and LRU caching. The prefetch horizon P(T_CPU) is the lookahead distance at which the worst-case stall time Tstall(x) <= Tdisk - x(T_CPU+T_hit+T_driver) reaches zero, roughly Tdisk/(T_CPU+T_hit+T_driver). This is derived assuming no disk congestion. Prefetching deeper gives no benefit, so prefetch buffers are capped at P(T_CPU). Kimbrel et al. model this as 'fixed horizon' with H = average disk read time / minimum block consumption time, and note that it stalls when disk bandwidth is too low.
result.corrections: No factual errors. All three works exist with the stated authors, venues and years. Nuances to keep the claim precise: (a) The 'backlog' that makes forestall aggressive is a predicted backlog. It is the number of missing blocks within a given distance in the hinted future reference string, each costing F time units (i*F >= d_i), not a measured disk-queue length. The paper puts it as 'estimation of upcoming disk load', and calls the regimes 'I/O-bound' vs 'compute-bound'. (b) Forestall is not only just-in-time. The implementation also keeps fixed horizon's within-H trigger (because of CSCAN reordering), uses an overestimate F' of F, and runs every prefetch through Cao et al.'s Do-No-Harm rule. (c) In Cao et al., Do No Harm is Rule 3 of four rules (with Optimal Prefetching, Optimal Replacement and First Opportunity), derived for a single-disk file cache. (d) The TIP horizon P(T_CPU) assumes no disk congestion or queueing and adequate bandwidth. It is a static lookahead depth, not a bandwidth-aware rule. The OSDI paper names 'fixed horizon' as TIP restricted to one hinting process. (e) The OSDI paper (1996) is in the ACM DL as 'Proceedings of the second USENIX symposium on Operating systems design and implementation'. Crossref dates it 1996-10-28.

Corrections:
1. **Dynamo also ships a related feature.** `agent_hints.speculative_prefill` warms the KV cache for the predicted next-turn prefix. It does this by recomputing (prefilling), not by loading from storage. The blog says it is "useful when the harness knows a tool call is about to return," so a novelty write-up should tell it apart from tier prefetch.
2. **"vLLM 'AgentX' " is a mislabel.** AgentX is SemiAnalysis's benchmark. The source is the blog post "vLLM x AgentX" (Sep 8, 2026). Its future work covers prefetch during inter-turn idle gaps "toward the worker likely to serve the next turn," plus a programmable prefetch interface. It does not describe a storage->GPU hook driven by predicted tool-return times. It only says hints could carry "tool-call latencies."
3. **"llm-d blog" names no post.** The best match is the P2P KV-sharing post (Aug 15, 2026). Its "What's Next" item pulls from local or remote CPU (not storage) "when a session's next request is predictable," not specifically on a predicted tool return.
4. **Only Dynamo is from April 2026.** The vLLM and llm-d sources are from July to September 2026.
